opus-5.5.text:
I think for me, issues and user feedback are really one of the most valuable signals you can get as a builder of open-source software. When you're developing something like XGBoost or TVM, you have your own picture in your head of how people are going to use it. But the moment it's out in the world, people bring it into settings you never imagined: different hardware, different data sizes, different workflows. The issues they file are basically a window into that reality.

So reviewing them regularly does a few things. First, it keeps you honest. A lot of times a bug report or a confusing question tells you that an abstraction you thought was clean actually isn't, or that the documentation assumes knowledge people don't have. Those are things you simply can't see from the inside.

Second, I find that the issues are often where the next research direction comes from. Some of the interesting problems we worked on, like supporting new hardware backends or making things run efficiently in distributed settings, started from users saying, "Hey, I'm trying to do this and it doesn't work." When you see the same kind of pain point come up again and again, that's a strong hint there's something fundamental worth solving.

And third, it's about the community. Open source isn't just code; it's people. When someone takes the time to write up an issue, responding thoughtfully tells them their contribution matters. Some of those people end up becoming contributors and even core maintainers later. Many of the strongest collaborators I've had started out by filing an issue or asking a question.

So for me it's less of a chore and more like a habit of listening. If you stop looking at what users are telling you, the project slowly drifts away from what people actually need. Staying close to that feedback is how you keep building something useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes user feedback as a valuable signal, but does not say that software’s success cannot be judged from its code at a single moment.

r002.rationale: It explains that regular feedback review helps identify bugs, unclear abstractions and documentation, and changing user needs, supporting continued work on the software.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the issues page is one of the most valuable things an open-source project has, and it's easy to underrate it. When we started XGBoost, and later TVM and MLC, I was building things based on my own picture of how people would use them. That picture is always incomplete. The moment real users show up, they bring workloads, hardware, data scales, and failure modes I never imagined. Issues are the cheapest possible way to see that.

A few concrete reasons I keep going back to them. First, bugs reported by users are usually bugs in my assumptions, not just in the code. Someone says "this is slow on my dataset," and when you dig in, you find a design choice that was fine for the datasets you tested on but breaks down at a different scale or sparsity pattern. That's information you can't get from your own benchmarks.

Second, feature requests tell you where the project's direction is actually pulling. If ten people independently ask for the same thing in slightly different words, that's a signal about where the field is going. A lot of what we built in TVM, for example, came from people asking "can I run this on this device" and us realizing there was a general abstraction hiding behind many specific requests.

Third, it keeps you honest about usability. As a maintainer you know all the workarounds, so you stop noticing the rough edges. A new user doesn't have that knowledge, and their confusion is a very precise map of where documentation or API design is failing.

And finally, it's about community. Open source only works if people feel heard. Responding to issues, even just acknowledging them, is how you turn a user into a contributor. Many of the core contributors to these projects started by filing an issue, then fixing it themselves. So reviewing feedback regularly isn't a chore on top of the real work. In a lot of ways, it is the real work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses user workloads, bugs, and design assumptions, but does not say that software’s success cannot be judged from its code at a single moment.

r002.rationale: It gives several reasons to review feedback regularly, but does not explain that issues are valuable because software requires ongoing maintenance.

astra-6.text: I think issues and user feedback help us understand where our assumptions differ from what people actually need. When we build something, we have certain use cases in mind, but users bring it into environments and applications we may not have considered. Sometimes a bug report reveals a deeper limitation in the design; sometimes a question tells us that the documentation is missing something. Reviewing that feedback regularly helps us identify recurring problems and prioritize improvements. It also creates a conversation with the community, where users can help shape the project and eventually become contributors themselves.

sol-6.1.text: I think issues and user feedback are a really important way to understand how people actually use the project. As developers, we have assumptions about what users need, but those assumptions are not always right. Someone might run into a problem we never anticipated, or use the system in a way that reveals a missing capability. Reviewing that feedback regularly helps us identify common pain points and decide where to focus. It also creates a conversation with the community, where users can help shape the project and potentially become contributors.
